physics.cosmos.big-bang-cmb.they-blamed-.title: They blamed the pigeons
physics.cosmos.big-bang-cmb.they-blamed-.hook: They cleaned the antenna, evicted the pigeons, and the hiss was still there. It was the oldest light in the universe.
physics.cosmos.big-bang-cmb.they-blamed-.author: author-physics-1
physics.cosmos.big-bang-cmb.they-blamed-.body:
In 1964 Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson had a beautiful horn antenna at Bell Labs in Holmdel, New Jersey, and a problem. Their receiver picked up a faint hiss that would not go away. It came from every direction of the sky, day and night, in every season — ruling out the Sun, the galaxy, New York City and every known radio source.

They spent months eliminating possibilities. They checked the electronics. They found pigeons nesting in the horn, evicted them, and scrubbed out what Penzias delicately called a white dielectric material. The hiss stayed: an excess antenna temperature of a few kelvin that no instrument fault could explain.

Thirty miles away at Princeton, Robert Dicke's group was building a detector to look for exactly this — the cooled afterglow of a hot early universe, predicted decades earlier and never seriously sought. A phone call, a visit, and the two groups published back-to-back in 1965: Princeton explaining what it meant, Bell Labs reporting a measurement, under a title that mentions only an excess antenna temperature.

They took the 1978 Nobel Prize for noise they had spent a year trying to remove.

recall.question: What is the cosmic microwave background, physically?
recall.answer: The light released when the universe cooled enough for electrons and nuclei to combine into neutral atoms, about 380,000 years after the Big Bang, so that photons could travel freely for the first time. It was a glow at roughly 3,000 K then; 13.8 billion years of expansion have stretched its wavelengths by a factor of about 1,100, cooling it to 2.725 K — microwaves, arriving from every direction at once.

physics.cosmos.dark-matter-energy.the-st.title: The stars at the edge are moving much too fast
physics.cosmos.dark-matter-energy.the-st.hook: The outer stars of a galaxy orbit as fast as the inner ones. By every rule we know, they should be flung off.
physics.cosmos.dark-matter-energy.the-st.author: author-physics-1
physics.cosmos.dark-matter-energy.the-st.body:
In the solar system, the further out you go the slower you orbit. Mercury takes 88 days, Neptune takes 165 years, and the relationship is exact: the Sun holds nearly all the mass, so orbital speed falls off as one over the square root of distance.

A galaxy looks like the same situation. Light concentrates in the middle, so the outskirts should crawl.

In 1970 Vera Rubin and Kent Ford measured the orbital speeds of glowing gas clouds across Andromeda, out past where the starlight fades. The speeds did not fall. They stayed flat, kilometre per second, all the way out — as if the mass kept accumulating in regions where nothing shines. Rubin found the same thing in galaxy after galaxy.

Fritz Zwicky had seen a version of it in 1933 in the Coma cluster and called the missing stuff *dunkle Materie*, and been largely ignored for forty years.

Something with mass is out there that neither emits nor absorbs light. We can weigh it, map it, and watch it bend light. We have no idea what it is.
physics.cosmos.dark-matter-energy.the-st.rigor:
For a test mass outside a spherical distribution, $\frac{mv^2}{r} = \frac{GM(r)m}{r^2}$, so

$$v(r) = \sqrt{\frac{GM(r)}{r}} .$$

If the mass is essentially all inside radius $r$, $M(r)$ is constant and $v \propto r^{-1/2}$ — the Keplerian fall-off. Flat curves, $v \approx$ const, instead require $M(r)\propto r$: mass growing linearly with radius, far beyond the visible disc, so the galaxy sits in a roughly isothermal halo of unseen material.

The evidence is no longer one measurement. Gravitational lensing weighs clusters independently of any dynamics and agrees. In the Bullet Cluster, two clusters passed through each other, the hot gas — most of the ordinary matter — was stripped and left behind, while the lensing mass went straight through with the galaxies, exactly as collisionless dark matter should. The CMB power spectrum's acoustic peaks independently fix the ratio of dark to ordinary matter.

Current accounting: about 5% ordinary matter, 27% dark matter, 68% dark energy, this last inferred from the 1998 supernova surveys showing the expansion is accelerating. Note the honest asymmetry: dark matter is a well-constrained *something* with unknown identity, while dark energy is mostly a name for a number in an equation.

recall.question: What do flat galactic rotation curves imply about the distribution of mass?

options.text: That gravity weakens at galactic distances.
options.why: that is the alternative hypothesis (modified gravity), and lensing plus the Bullet Cluster weigh heavily against it.

options.text: That the enclosed mass keeps growing roughly linearly with radius, far beyond where the light stops.
options.why: $v\approx$ const forces $M(r)\propto r$.

options.text: That the stars are not gravitationally bound to the galaxy.
options.why: they plainly are; they have completed many orbits without escaping.

options.text: That the galaxy's centre holds more mass than we can see.
options.why: extra mass in the centre would steepen the fall-off, not flatten it.

sources.title: Rotation of the Andromeda Nebula from a Spectroscopic Survey of Emission Regions
sources.author: Vera C. Rubin & W. Kent Ford Jr.

physics.cosmos.higgs.the-higgs-gives-you.title: The Higgs gives you about one percent of your mass
physics.cosmos.higgs.the-higgs-gives-you.hook: The Higgs field is described as the thing that gives matter mass. It is responsible for about one percent of yours.
physics.cosmos.higgs.the-higgs-gives-you.author: author-physics-1
physics.cosmos.higgs.the-higgs-gives-you.body:
On 4 July 2012, CERN announced a new particle at about 125 GeV, and the press explained that physicists had finally found the thing that gives everything its mass. That explanation is off by two orders of magnitude for you personally.

Almost all your mass is protons and neutrons. Almost none of *their* mass is the mass of the quarks inside them. Three quarks account for roughly one percent of a proton's mass; the other ninety-nine percent is the energy of the gluon field binding them and the kinetic energy of the quarks rattling around inside. By $E = mc^2$, that energy weighs. You are, to a very good approximation, made of confined energy.

What the Higgs field does do is give mass to the *elementary* particles — electrons, quarks, and crucially the $W$ and $Z$ bosons — and that matters enormously. Without it the electron would be massless, atoms would not exist, and there would be nothing to bind.

So the headline was wrong about the number and right about the stakes.
physics.cosmos.higgs.the-higgs-gives-you.rigor:
Start with a complex scalar field and a potential shaped like a sombrero:

$$V(\phi) = -\mu^2|\phi|^2 + \lambda|\phi|^4, \qquad \mu^2,\lambda > 0 .$$

The Lagrangian is symmetric under $\phi\to e^{i\theta}\phi$, but the minimum is not at $\phi=0$; it lies on a circle $|\phi| = v/\sqrt2$ with $v \approx 246$ GeV. The field must pick a point on that circle, so the *state* breaks a symmetry the *laws* retain — spontaneous symmetry breaking. Expand around the chosen minimum and the radial excitation is a massive scalar: the Higgs boson.

Gauge that symmetry and the would-be massless angular mode is eaten by the gauge field, which acquires $m_W = \tfrac12 g v$. Fermions get mass from Yukawa terms $-y_f\bar\psi\phi\psi \to -\tfrac{y_f v}{\sqrt2}\bar\psi\psi$, so $m_f = y_f v/\sqrt2$: the Higgs supplies the mechanism, but each $y_f$ is a free parameter, which is why the theory cannot predict the electron's mass.

The other ninety-nine percent is quantum chromodynamics. The proton's mass comes out of the QCD scale $\Lambda_{\mathrm{QCD}} \sim 200$ MeV generated by the running of the strong coupling — mass from a dimensionless theory with no mass put in, which is arguably the more remarkable of the two mechanisms.

recall.question: Where does most of the mass of a proton come from?

options.text: From the masses of its three quarks.
options.why: they contribute roughly one percent of the total.

options.text: From the energy of the gluon field and the quarks' motion inside it, converted by $E=mc^2$.
options.why: confinement energy is what a proton mostly weighs.

options.text: From the Higgs field acting on the proton as a whole.
options.why: the Higgs couples to elementary particles, not to composites.

options.text: From the binding energy of the electrons around the nucleus.
options.why: atomic binding energies are smaller by a factor of roughly a million.

physics.cosmos.neutrinos.dear-radioactiv.title: Dear radioactive ladies and gentlemen
physics.cosmos.neutrinos.dear-radioactiv.hook: Pauli invented a particle to save conservation of energy, admitted it might be undetectable, and skipped the meeting for a ball.
physics.cosmos.neutrinos.dear-radioactiv.author: author-physics-1
physics.cosmos.neutrinos.dear-radioactiv.body:
Beta decay had a scandal. A nucleus emits an electron and turns into a different nucleus, and in a two-body split the electron's energy is fixed by arithmetic. Measured, it came out with a *range* of energies, nearly always less than the books demanded. Bohr was willing to abandon conservation of energy inside the nucleus.

On 4 December 1930 Pauli wrote to a meeting in Tübingen he was not attending — he was staying in Zurich for a ball — opening "Dear radioactive ladies and gentlemen". He proposed what he called a desperate remedy: a neutral, very light particle emitted alongside the electron, carrying off the missing energy unseen. He conceded that such a thing might never be detected, and that nothing ventured was nothing gained.

It took twenty-six years. Cowan and Reines caught neutrinos beside a nuclear reactor in 1956.

Right now, about 65 billion of them from the Sun are passing through every square centimetre of you, every second, and essentially none of them notice you are there.
physics.cosmos.neutrinos.dear-radioactiv.rigor:
The decay is $n \to p + e^- + \bar\nu_e$, a three-body final state, so the electron energy is distributed continuously between zero and the endpoint instead of taking a single value. That continuous spectrum was the anomaly; the third body is the explanation.

Neutrinos are hard to see because they feel only the weak interaction. A typical cross-section at MeV energies is around $10^{-44}\ \mathrm{cm^2}$, which for the solar flux gives a mean free path in lead measured in light years. Reines and Cowan won by brute force: a reactor flux of $\sim10^{13}$ per cm² per second, a target of several hundred litres, and a coincidence signature — inverse beta decay $\bar\nu_e + p \to n + e^+$ gives two annihilation photons promptly and a neutron capture microseconds later.

Then the second surprise. Solar neutrino detectors saw only a third of the predicted rate for thirty years. Super-Kamiokande (1998) and SNO (2001) showed why: neutrinos change flavour in flight. Oscillation requires the mass eigenstates to differ from the flavour eigenstates and to propagate with different phases, which requires nonzero mass — flatly contradicting the Standard Model as written. It remains the only laboratory evidence of physics beyond it.

recall.question: What did the continuous energy spectrum of beta decay reveal?

options.text: That energy is not conserved in nuclear processes.
options.why: Bohr's guess, and wrong; conservation survived intact.

options.text: That a third, unseen particle must be sharing the energy, making the decay a three-body process.
options.why: in a two-body decay the electron's energy would be a single fixed value.

options.text: That electrons are emitted with random energies by an unknown mechanism.
options.why: "random" was the observation; the point is that it required an extra participant.

options.text: That the nucleus contains electrons of varying energy.
options.why: nuclei contain no electrons; the electron is created in the decay.

physics.cosmos.nuclear.iron-is-where-the.title: Iron is where the energy runs out
physics.cosmos.nuclear.iron-is-where-the.hook: Fusion and fission release energy for the same reason, and they run in opposite directions. The turning point is iron.
physics.cosmos.nuclear.iron-is-where-the.author: author-physics-1
physics.cosmos.nuclear.iron-is-where-the.body:
A helium nucleus weighs less than the two protons and two neutrons it is made of. Not slightly less by accident — reliably less, by about 0.7% of the total. The missing mass left as energy when the pieces bound together, and $E=mc^2$ converts the shortfall into the number.

Plot that shortfall per nucleon against the size of the nucleus and you get one of the most consequential curves in science. It rises steeply from hydrogen, peaks around iron and nickel, and declines slowly toward uranium.

Everything follows from the shape. Below the peak, joining light nuclei moves you uphill and releases energy: that is fusion, and it is what the Sun does. Above the peak, splitting heavy nuclei also moves you uphill: that is fission, and it is what a reactor does. Two opposite processes, one explanation.

The peak is why stars die. A star fusing its way up the curve reaches iron and finds no further energy available — the fire has nothing left to burn, and the core collapses in about a second.
physics.cosmos.nuclear.iron-is-where-the.rigor:
Binding energy is the mass defect, $B = (Zm_p + Nm_n - m_{\text{nucleus}})c^2$, and the curve plots $B/A$ against mass number $A$. It peaks near $^{56}\mathrm{Fe}$ and $^{62}\mathrm{Ni}$ at about 8.8 MeV per nucleon.

Why a peak at all? Two effects fight. The strong force is short-ranged, so each nucleon binds only to its neighbours and $B/A$ saturates; the electrostatic repulsion between protons is long-ranged and grows like $Z^2/A^{1/3}$. Small nuclei lose to surface effects, large ones lose to Coulomb repulsion, and the optimum lands near $A\approx56$.

Now the numbers that matter. Hydrogen fusion converts about $0.7\%$ of the input mass to energy; uranium fission about $0.09\%$. Per kilogram, fusion wins by roughly a factor of eight — and both beat chemistry by a factor of ten million, because nuclear binding energies are measured in MeV and chemical bonds in eV.

The price is the barrier. Two nuclei must reach $\sim10^{-15}$ m against a Coulomb repulsion that needs hundreds of keV, while the Sun's core sits at only about 1.3 keV. Fusion proceeds anyway, by quantum tunnelling through the barrier, in the exponentially rare tail of the Boltzmann distribution. The Sun runs on the fact that rare is not never.

recall.question: Why do both fusion of light nuclei and fission of heavy nuclei release energy?

options.text: Because both split atoms into smaller pieces.
options.why: fusion does the opposite; it merges them.

options.text: Because binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron, so moving toward the peak from either side releases the difference.
options.why: one curve, two directions, same rule.

options.text: Because heavy nuclei are unstable and light nuclei are stable.
options.why: stability is not the criterion; iron is stable and yields nothing either way.

options.text: Because fission releases neutrons and fusion absorbs them.
options.why: neutron bookkeeping matters for chain reactions, not for where the energy comes from.

physics.cosmos.standard-model.everything.title: Everything you have ever touched is three particles
physics.cosmos.standard-model.everything.hook: Every object you have ever held is built from three particles. The Standard Model contains seventeen, and nobody knows why.
physics.cosmos.standard-model.everything.author: author-physics-1

reviewed.notes: Reconciled the headline seventeen particles with the twelve gauge bosons in the rigor: species versus states.

physics.cosmos.standard-model.everything.body:
Your hands, this screen, the air, the Andes, the Sun: up quarks, down quarks, electrons. Three protons' worth of ingredients. Two ups and a down make a proton, two downs and an up make a neutron, electrons do the chemistry. Add photons so you can see it and the inventory of ordinary experience is complete.

The Standard Model has seventeen particles, and the surplus is the strange part. There is a second copy of those building blocks — heavier, unstable, otherwise identical — and then a third copy, heavier still. Nothing needs them. When the muon turned up in cosmic rays, a heavier twin of the electron with no job to do, I. I. Rabi is remembered for asking who ordered that.

Nobody has answered. Three generations, spanning at least eleven orders of magnitude in mass from the neutrinos to the top quark, and the theory that describes them cannot predict a single one of those masses.

The Standard Model is the most successful theory in physics and an unfinished sentence.
physics.cosmos.standard-model.everything.rigor:
Content: three generations of $(u,d)$-type quarks and $(e,\nu_e)$-type leptons; twelve gauge bosons for the group $SU(3)_C\times SU(2)_L\times U(1)_Y$ — eight gluons, $W^{\pm}$, $Z^0$, photon — and one Higgs scalar. The headline "seventeen" counts species rather than states: the eight gluons count once between them, as do $W^+$ and $W^-$.

The forces are not extra assumptions. Demand that the Lagrangian be invariant under *local* transformations of that group, and the gauge fields are forced on you, along with their couplings to matter — the same trade the group-theory card described, symmetry in, structure out.

The embarrassment is the parameter count. Roughly nineteen numbers must be measured and inserted by hand: nine charged-fermion masses, three quark mixing angles plus a CP-violating phase, three gauge couplings, two Higgs parameters, and the strong CP angle. Neutrino masses and mixings add about seven more. None is predicted; the electron-to-top mass ratio alone spans five orders of magnitude with no explanation.

And the model is knowingly incomplete: it excludes gravity, provides no dark-matter candidate, and gives no mechanism for the matter–antimatter asymmetry that lets any of this exist. It has nonetheless survived every collider test attempted, which is the frustrating part.

recall.question: What do the second and third generations of matter particles contribute to ordinary matter?

options.text: They make up the nuclei of heavier elements.
options.why: every nucleus, from hydrogen to uranium, is built from first-generation up and down quarks.

options.text: Nothing: they are unstable heavier copies that decay quickly, and ordinary matter needs only the first generation.
options.why: why nature includes them at all is an open question.

options.text: They mediate the strong and weak forces.
options.why: forces are carried by gauge bosons, which are a separate part of the inventory.

options.text: They account for dark matter.
options.why: they decay in microseconds or less; dark matter has to be stable over billions of years.

physics.cosmos.standard-model.one-family.title: One family of particles is named after a man a journal turned down
physics.cosmos.standard-model.one-family.hook: Every particle is either a loner or a joiner. The joiners are named after a man whose paper a journal turned down.
physics.cosmos.standard-model.one-family.author: author-physics-1

reviewed.notes: Title said the family is named after a rejected paper; bosons are named after Bose, so retitled to 'named after a man a journal turned down' (id unchanged). Facts verified: Reader at Dhaka since 1921, no doctorate, Phil. Mag. rejection, Einstein's translation.

physics.cosmos.standard-model.one-family.body:
In 1924 Satyendra Nath Bose, a reader at the new University of Dhaka with no doctorate, mailed a short paper to Einstein. The *Philosophical Magazine* had already turned it down. Einstein translated it into German himself and got it published.

Bose had counted particles of light as if no two could ever be told apart. That counting has a consequence: such particles happily crowd into the same state. Laser light is that crowd.

Electrons obey the opposite rule, Pauli's: never two in one state. Every particle in the Standard Model is one kind or the other. The loners, called fermions (quarks, electrons, neutrinos), make matter. The joiners, named bosons after Bose, are the force carriers and the Higgs.

recall.question: What separates the two families of particles?

options.text: Their mass: bosons are the heavy ones.
options.why: the photon is a massless boson and the top quark is a very heavy loner.

options.text: Whether two of them can share the same state.
options.why: loners (fermions) never can, joiners (bosons) crowd in freely.

options.text: Their charge: bosons are neutral.
options.why: the W boson carries charge, and the neutrino is a neutral loner.

physics.cosmos.standard-model.split-in-t.title: Split in two, the pieces have no choice
physics.cosmos.standard-model.split-in-t.hook: Break something into two pieces and their energies are fixed by arithmetic. Beta decay broke that rule, unless a piece was missing.
physics.cosmos.standard-model.split-in-t.author: author-physics-1

reviewed.notes: Alpha line now says 'from a given decay' (alpha fine structure gives several sharp lines per nucleus); rigor states E = sqrt(m^2+p^2) instead of assuming relativity; Bohr distractor's why now teaches the endpoint argument. Diagram checked in light and dark: correct and legible.

physics.cosmos.standard-model.split-in-t.body:
If a break-up always launches a given fragment at the same speed, there were two pieces. If the speeds smear, there were more, seen or not.

Take a cannon. Ball one way, cannon recoiling the other: their momenta must cancel, and the energy released is fixed, so there is exactly one way to share it. Every two-piece decay works like this, which is why alpha particles from a given decay share one energy.

Beta electrons come out with any energy from nearly zero up to a ceiling. With three pieces, momentum can balance in endlessly many ways, so energy splits endlessly many ways. The cannon is slow and electrons are not, but relativity changes the arithmetic, not the count.
physics.cosmos.standard-model.split-in-t.rigor:
The count, made exact. Use units with $c=1$. A particle of mass $M$ at rest decays into masses $m_1, m_2$. Momentum conservation forces $\vec p_1 = -\vec p_2$, so both have the same $|\vec p| = p$. A piece of mass $m$ carries energy $\sqrt{m^2+p^2}$, so energy conservation reads

$$M = \sqrt{m_1^2+p^2} + \sqrt{m_2^2+p^2}.$$

The right side is strictly increasing in $p$, equals $m_1+m_2 < M$ at $p=0$ and grows without bound, so by the intermediate value theorem there is exactly one $p$. Since $E_1^2-E_2^2 = m_1^2-m_2^2$ and $E_1+E_2 = M$, dividing gives $E_1-E_2$, hence

$$E_1 = \frac{M^2+m_1^2-m_2^2}{2M}.$$

One number: a spike. That is the cannon's single speed.

With three bodies, $\vec p_1+\vec p_2+\vec p_3 = 0$ only says three vectors close a triangle, and energy adds one more equation. A continuum of solutions remains. The electron's energy runs from $m_e$ (at rest, the other two back to back) to a maximum reached when the other two fly off together, with invariant mass $m_2+m_3$:

$$E_{\max} = \frac{M^2+m_e^2-(m_2+m_3)^2}{2M}.$$

For the free neutron the measured kinetic-energy ceiling is $0.782$ MeV, and the smear fills everything below it.

recall.question: Why does a smear of electron energies point to an unseen third particle?

options.text: Because energy is only conserved on average in nuclei.
options.why: that was Bohr's fallback, but the smear stops at a sharp ceiling equal to the full energy released, exactly where strict conservation says it must.

options.text: Because two pieces must share the energy one fixed way; only three or more can share it in a continuum of ways.
options.why: momentum balance plus fixed energy leaves one solution for two bodies and a whole family for three.

options.text: Because electrons lose different amounts of energy on the way out of the atom.
options.why: calorimeter experiments in 1927 and 1930 ruled this out: the missing energy never showed up as heat.

physics.cosmos.standard-model.the-neutri.title: The neutrino was first called the neutron
physics.cosmos.standard-model.the-neutri.hook: Pauli named his invisible particle the neutron, because the neutron had not been discovered yet.
physics.cosmos.standard-model.the-neutri.author: author-physics-1

reviewed.notes: First sentence restated the title and hook; rewrote it to give the reason the name was free. Nitrogen 14p+7e and Pauli's 'neutron' checked against Ecker (arXiv:2007.06926) and Pauli's letter.

physics.cosmos.standard-model.the-neutri.body:
When Pauli proposed his invisible particle in 1930, the name was up for grabs: the heavy neutron had not been found. Physicists pictured a nucleus as protons with electrons packed in (nitrogen: fourteen protons, seven electrons), so beta decay looked like a nucleus letting an electron out.

Chadwick found the heavy neutron in 1932. In Rome, Fermi's circle nicknamed Pauli's particle the *neutrino*, "little neutral one", and Fermi's 1933–34 theory made the real shift: the electron was never inside. It is created when a neutron turns into a proton.

recall.question: Where does the electron in beta decay come from?

options.text: It was stored in the nucleus all along.
options.why: the pre-1932 picture; nuclei contain no electrons.

options.text: It is created on the spot, when a neutron turns into a proton.
options.why: Fermi's move: particles can be made and destroyed, not just released.

options.text: It is knocked out of the atom's outer shell.
options.why: shell electrons can be ejected by other processes, but the beta electron is brand new.

physics.cosmos.standard-model.the-weak-f.title: The weak force is not weak
physics.cosmos.standard-model.the-weak-f.hook: By its basic coupling, the weak force is no weaker than electromagnetism. Its problem is the weight of its messenger.
physics.cosmos.standard-model.the-weak-f.author: author-physics-1

reviewed.notes: Tong URL moved to its canonical host (the DAMTP link 301-redirects and failed the link checker). 'Almost five times' is Tong's own wording: alpha_W = g^2/4pi ~ 1/30 vs alpha ~ 1/137.

physics.cosmos.standard-model.the-weak-f.body: By its basic coupling, the weak force is at least as strong as electromagnetism; by one standard measure, almost five times stronger. It looks feeble because of its messenger: the W boson weighs about 86 protons. A decaying neutron has about 1.3 MeV to spend, and a real W costs 80,000. So the decay runs through a W that never becomes real, and a free neutron lasts about fifteen minutes. Neutrinos, which feel only this force and gravity, cross the whole Earth for the same reason.

recall.question: Why does a free neutron take about fifteen minutes to decay?

options.text: Because the weak force's basic coupling is tiny.
options.why: it is at least as big as electromagnetism's.

options.text: Because its messenger, the W, is enormously heavier than the energy the decay has to spend.
options.why: so the decay can only run through a W that never becomes real, which is rare.

options.text: Because gluons hold the neutron's quarks too tightly.
options.why: gluons bind quarks, but only the weak force can turn a down quark into an up.

physics.cosmos.standard-model.two-prison.title: Two prisoners and a thermometer
physics.cosmos.standard-model.two-prison.hook: Chadwick spent the war in a racecourse stable, where he turned a stranded army cadet into the man who proved energy was vanishing.
physics.cosmos.standard-model.two-prison.author: author-physics-1
physics.cosmos.standard-model.two-prison.body:
In 1914 James Chadwick showed that beta-decay electrons leave with a smear of energies, not one. Then war broke out, and he spent four years interned at Ruhleben, a racecourse near Berlin. In a horse stable he set up a lab with a fellow prisoner, Charles Ellis, a cadet caught on holiday, who left the army for physics.

Lise Meitner disagreed: the electrons must leave with one energy and lose some on the way out. In 1927 Ellis and William Wooster caught every electron in a calorimeter and measured the heat. It matched the smear's average, not its top. Meitner redid it more carefully and agreed.

The energy was really gone, unless something unseen was carrying it off.

recall.question: What did the 1927 calorimeter settle?

options.text: That electrons leave with one energy and lose some on the way out.
options.why: that was Meitner's view; if it were true, the heat would have matched the top of the smear.

options.text: That the energy is missing at the source: the heat matched the smear's average, so nothing was hiding as heat.
options.why: which left two options, give up energy conservation or find what was carrying it away.

options.text: That energy conservation fails in nuclei.
options.why: the experiment showed the energy was missing, not why; Pauli's unseen particle was the other explanation.

sources.author: Gerhard Ecker

physics.cosmos.standard-model.yukawa-wei.title: Yukawa weighed a particle nobody had seen
physics.cosmos.standard-model.yukawa-wei.hook: Yukawa guessed a particle's weight from the size of a nucleus. A 22-year-old Brazilian clinched it on a Bolivian mountain.
physics.cosmos.standard-model.yukawa-wei.author: author-physics-1

reviewed.notes: Hook said Lattes 'found it' on Chacaltaya; the first two pi-mu events (Nature, 24 May 1947) came from Occhialini's Pic du Midi plates, and Lattes's April 1947 Chacaltaya plates added ~30 that settled it. Hook now says 'clinched'. Body already accurate.

physics.cosmos.standard-model.yukawa-wei.body:
In 1935 Hideki Yukawa predicted a particle's mass from the size of a nucleus. His rule: forces travel by messenger, and a heavy messenger can't go far. The nuclear force dies within a nucleus's width, so its messenger should weigh about 200 times an electron.

In 1936 cosmic rays delivered one of nearly that mass. Wrong one: the muon, which barely touched nuclei. The real messenger, the pion, turned up in 1947 in photographic plates exposed on mountaintops, among them 5,200 metres up Chacaltaya, Bolivia, where a 22-year-old Brazilian, César Lattes, carried them.

Yukawa and Cecil Powell, the group's leader, got Nobels. Lattes, first author of the discovery paper, didn't. Brazil named its database of researchers' CVs after him.

recall.question: How could Yukawa estimate the mass of a particle nobody had seen?

options.text: A heavier messenger reaches less far, and the nuclear force reaches only about a nucleus's width.
options.why: so the force's short reach set the messenger's weight.

options.text: He weighed cosmic-ray tracks.
options.why: the tracks came later, and the first candidate, the muon, was the wrong particle.

options.text: He added up the masses of the quarks inside it.
options.why: quarks were not proposed until 1964; the pion's quark content came long after.

sources.title: Processes Involving Charged Mesons
sources.author: C. M. G. Lattes, H. Muirhead, G. P. S. Occhialini, C. F. Powell

physics.cosmos.stars.el-sol-es-peor-reac.title: ¿Cuánta potencia produce un metro cúbico del centro del Sol?
physics.cosmos.stars.el-sol-es-peor-reac.hook: El centro del Sol produce menos calor por metro cúbico que una pila de compost. Y sin embargo ahí está.
physics.cosmos.stars.el-sol-es-peor-reac.author: author-physics-1

reviewed.notes: 276.5 W/m3 is the peak at the centre. Dropped the unverified reptile comparison; added that the core is 1.5% of the volume and the whole-Sun average is 0.27 W/m3.

physics.cosmos.stars.el-sol-es-peor-reac.body:
El Sol entrega $3{,}8\times10^{26}$ vatios. Su núcleo está a 15 millones de kelvin y ahí ocurre la fusión: cuatro protones se convierten en un núcleo de helio, y la diferencia de masa sale como energía.

Con esos números, adivina antes de seguir: un metro cúbico del centro del Sol, el punto más caliente y denso de todo el sistema solar, ¿cuánta potencia produce? ¿Un megavatio? ¿Mil? ¿Un reactor nuclear entero?

Pista incómoda: la fusión protón-protón depende de que dos protones se acerquen lo suficiente venciendo su repulsión eléctrica, y a 1,3 keV de energía térmica eso casi nunca pasa. Ocurre solo por efecto túnel, en la cola exponencial de la distribución de Boltzmann. Un protón cualquiera del núcleo espera, en promedio, miles de millones de años antes de fusionarse.

Lo que hace al Sol brillante no es que sea intenso. Es que es enorme.

recall.question: ¿Cuál es la densidad de potencia en el centro del Sol?
recall.answer: Unos 276,5 vatios por metro cúbico en el punto central: aproximadamente lo mismo que una pila de compost. Y eso es el máximo. La producción cae rápido hacia afuera —el núcleo es apenas un 1,5% del volumen solar—, así que repartida sobre los $1{,}4\times10^{27}$ metros cúbicos del Sol la densidad media es de $0{,}27$ W/m³. El Sol brilla por tamaño, no por intensidad. Esa lentitud es una suerte: si la fusión fuera eficiente, el Sol habría gastado su hidrógeno hace miles de millones de años y nosotros no estaríamos aquí.

physics.em.charge-fields.one-percent-mor.title: What if you had one percent more electrons than your friend?
physics.em.charge-fields.one-percent-mor.hook: Matter is electrically neutral to absurd precision. Break that by one percent and the numbers stop being human.
physics.em.charge-fields.one-percent-mor.author: author-physics-1
physics.em.charge-fields.one-percent-mor.body:
Between two protons, the electric repulsion is about $10^{36}$ times the gravitational attraction. Thirty-six orders of magnitude. Electricity is not a slightly stronger force than gravity; it is a different kind of large.

So why does gravity run the universe while electricity mostly sits quiet? Because matter cancels itself out. Every atom carries exactly as many electrons as protons, and the two charges are equal to better than one part in $10^{20}$. Bulk matter is neutral, and neutral is boring.

Here is the estimate. You are made of roughly $2\times10^{28}$ electrons. Suppose you had one percent more of them than protons, and so did a friend standing a metre away. Both of you are now negative by the same amount.

How hard do you push each other apart? Guess before you look — and compare it to something you can picture, like the weight of a mountain.

recall.question: How large is the repulsion between two people a metre apart, each carrying one percent excess electrons?
recall.answer: Around $10^{25}$ newtons. One percent of $2\times10^{28}$ electrons is a charge of about $3\times10^{7}$ coulombs each, and $F = kq^2/r^2 \approx 9\times10^{9}\times(3\times10^{7})^2 \approx 10^{25}$ N. Mount Everest weighs about $10^{16}$ N, so this is a billion Everests — a good fraction of what it would take to lift the Earth. Feynman ran the same estimate in 1964 and landed in the same place. That is why matter bothers to be neutral.

sources.title: The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Vol. II, Ch. 1: Electromagnetism
sources.author: Richard Feynman

physics.em.circuits.los-electrones-van-a.title: Los electrones van a paso de caracol y la luz se prende ya
physics.em.circuits.los-electrones-van-a.hook: Los electrones en el cable de tu lámpara avanzan más lento que un caracol. La luz se prende de todos modos al instante.
physics.em.circuits.los-electrones-van-a.author: author-physics-1
physics.em.circuits.los-electrones-van-a.body:
Prendes el interruptor y el bombillo se enciende sin demora perceptible. La explicación obvia —los electrones corren por el cable hasta el bombillo— es falsa por varios órdenes de magnitud.

En un cable de cobre normal, con un amperio de corriente, cada electrón avanza a unos $0{,}07$ milímetros por segundo. Más lento que un caracol. Si el encendido dependiera de que un electrón viaje del interruptor al bombillo, tendrías que esperar horas.

Lo que sí viaja rápido es el campo eléctrico: se establece a lo largo del cable a una fracción grande de la velocidad de la luz. Los electrones ya estaban ahí, repartidos por todo el conductor; el campo simplemente les avisa, casi simultáneamente, que empiecen a arrastrarse.

La analogía útil es una manguera ya llena de agua. Abres la llave y sale agua por el otro extremo de inmediato, aunque ninguna molécula haya recorrido la manguera. Donde falla: en el cable no hay nada incompresible empujando; lo que se propaga es un campo.
physics.em.circuits.los-electrones-van-a.rigor:
La velocidad de arrastre sale de contar portadores. Si hay $n$ electrones libres por metro cúbico, cada uno con carga $q$, en un cable de sección $A$:

$$I = nqAv_d \quad\Longrightarrow\quad v_d = \frac{I}{nqA}.$$

Para el cobre $n \approx 8{,}5\times10^{28}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$. Con $I = 1$ A y $A = 1\ \mathrm{mm^2} = 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m^2}$:

$$v_d = \frac{1}{(8{,}5\times10^{28})(1{,}6\times10^{-19})(10^{-6})} \approx 7\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m/s}.$$

Setenta micras por segundo. Mientras tanto, la perturbación electromagnética recorre el cable a $v = c/\sqrt{\varepsilon_r\mu_r}$, típicamente entre $0{,}6c$ y $0{,}9c$.

Y hay una vuelta de tuerca que incomoda a todo el mundo la primera vez: la energía no viaja *dentro* del cable. El vector de Poynting $\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{H}$ apunta hacia adentro del conductor desde el espacio que lo rodea. La energía fluye por el campo alrededor del cable y entra lateralmente; el cobre sirve de guía, no de tubería. El caracol nunca fue el mensajero.

recall.question: ¿Por qué se enciende el bombillo casi al instante si los electrones se arrastran tan lento?

options.text: Porque los electrones aceleran hasta casi la velocidad de la luz al cerrar el circuito.
options.why: chocan con la red del metal constantemente; su velocidad media de arrastre se queda en micras por segundo.

options.text: Porque lo que se propaga es el campo electromagnético, y los electrones ya estaban repartidos por todo el cable.
options.why: el campo los pone en movimiento casi simultáneamente en toda su longitud.

options.text: Porque la corriente alterna no necesita que los electrones se desplacen.
options.why: también ocurre en corriente continua, donde sí hay desplazamiento neto.

options.text: Porque el cable es muy corto y la distancia no importa.
options.why: funciona igual con cables de kilómetros, con un retardo de microsegundos.

physics.em.light-optics.why-the-sky-is-b.title: Why the sky is blue — and why that's only two thirds of the answer
physics.em.light-optics.why-the-sky-is-b.hook: Violet scatters more than blue. So why isn't the sky violet? The honest answer needs two extra facts, and both are about you.
physics.em.light-optics.why-the-sky-is-b.author: author-physics-1

reviewed.notes: Body claimed blue scatters nine times more than red; nine is the violet-to-red ratio. Reworded to agree with the rigor.

physics.em.light-optics.why-the-sky-is-b.body:
Sunlight arrives white. Air is transparent. Yet the sky away from the sun glows blue, which means air is doing something wavelength-dependent to light that is not simply letting it pass.

It scatters it. A molecule in the path of a light wave has its electrons jiggled by the wave's electric field, and a jiggling charge radiates in all directions. The efficiency of that re-radiation depends brutally on wavelength: short waves jiggle faster, and the power radiated goes as the fourth power of frequency. The blue end of the band is scattered several times more than the red. Look anywhere except at the sun and you are seeing sunlight that bounced, which means you are seeing mostly the blue end.

Two honest footnotes. Violet scatters *more* than blue, so why not a violet sky? Because sunlight contains less violet to begin with, and because your cone cells register the scattered mixture as blue with white mixed in. And at sunset the beam travels a long slanted path through air, losing its blue on the way, so what survives to reach you directly is red.
physics.em.light-optics.why-the-sky-is-b.rigor:
Model each molecule as an induced dipole: $\mathbf{p} = \alpha\mathbf{E}_0 e^{-i\omega t}$. An oscillating dipole radiates total power

$$P = \frac{\omega^4 |p|^2}{12\pi\varepsilon_0 c^3},$$

so the scattering cross-section goes as $\sigma \propto \omega^4 \propto \lambda^{-4}$. That single exponent is the whole phenomenon. The ratio between the violet and red ends of the visible band is

$$\left(\frac{700\ \mathrm{nm}}{400\ \mathrm{nm}}\right)^4 \approx 9.4 .$$

Three conditions have to hold for this to be Rayleigh scattering rather than something else: the scatterer must be much smaller than $\lambda$ (a nitrogen molecule is about $0.3$ nm against $500$ nm), it must be non-absorbing, and the scatterers must be positioned randomly — a perfect crystal of air would not scatter at all, because the re-radiated waves would cancel in every direction except forward. What you are seeing overhead is *density fluctuation*, which is why the brightness of the sky is, in principle, a measurement of how many molecules a cubic metre of air contains.

And when the particles are *not* small compared to $\lambda$ — water droplets in a cloud, at micrometre scale — the $\lambda^{-4}$ law fails entirely and you get Mie scattering, which is white. That is why clouds are grey and the sky between them is blue.

recall.question: Violet light scatters more strongly than blue. Why is the daytime sky blue rather than violet?

options.text: Violet light is absorbed by ozone before it reaches us.
options.why: some ultraviolet is, but visible violet reaches the ground fine.

options.text: Sunlight contains less violet than blue, and human colour vision reports the scattered mixture as blue plus white.
options.why: the physics favours violet; the source spectrum and your eye outvote it.

options.text: Violet scatters so much that it never reaches the observer.
options.why: scattered light is precisely what reaches you when you look away from the sun.

options.text: Because air molecules resonate at blue wavelengths.
options.why: there is no resonance in the visible; the $\lambda^{-4}$ law is smooth across the whole band.

sources.title: Absorption and Scattering of Light by Small Particles
sources.author: Craig F. Bohren & Donald R. Huffman

physics.em.magnetism-induction.faradays-.title: The twitch that became the entire electrical grid
physics.em.magnetism-induction.faradays-.hook: Faraday's needle only moved when he connected the battery and when he disconnected it. Steady current did nothing at all.
physics.em.magnetism-induction.faradays-.author: author-physics-1
physics.em.magnetism-induction.faradays-.body:
On 29 August 1831 Michael Faraday wound two separate coils of wire on opposite sides of an iron ring. One coil went to a battery, the other to a galvanometer. The coils never touched. He closed the battery circuit and the galvanometer needle jumped — then fell back to zero while current kept flowing steadily. He opened the circuit and the needle jumped the other way.

That is the whole discovery, and the important part is the part that looks like failure. A steady magnetic field does nothing. Only *change* induces a current. Faraday's ring is a transformer, the device that makes long-distance power distribution possible and the reason your wall socket carries alternating current: alternating means always changing, and change is the only thing induction responds to.

Faraday had almost no mathematics. He thought in pictures, and invented field lines because he needed something to draw. Maxwell's later achievement was largely to take those lines seriously enough to write them down.

Here is the law in the form Faraday could not have written.
physics.em.magnetism-induction.faradays-.rigor:
$$\oint_{\partial\Sigma}\mathbf{E}\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell = -\frac{d}{dt}\int_\Sigma \mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{A} = -\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt}.$$

Read it as: a changing magnetic flux through a loop drives an electromotive force around the loop. For $N$ turns the flux is counted $N$ times, $\mathcal{E} = -N\,d\Phi_B/dt$. A 200-turn coil of area $0.01\ \mathrm{m^2}$ in a field ramping by $0.5$ T in $0.1$ s gives $\mathcal{E} = 200\times0.01\times5 = 10$ V — a lab-bench number from lab-bench quantities.

The minus sign is the physics. Lenz's law says the induced current opposes the change that produced it, and the reason is conservation of energy: if the induced current reinforced the change, a nudge would amplify itself and you would have a machine that the previous card's patent examiner would refuse to read about. Push a magnet toward a coil and the coil pushes back; the work you do against that push is exactly the electrical energy you get out.

Note the structural point. Faraday's law is the statement that $\mathbf{E}$ is *not* a gradient field when $\mathbf{B}$ changes: $\oint\mathbf{E}\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell \ne 0$, so no potential function exists. Electrostatics is the special case where the right-hand side vanishes.

recall.question: Why did Faraday's galvanometer read zero while a steady current flowed in the first coil?

options.text: Because iron blocks a constant magnetic field.
options.why: iron channels the field; a steady field was certainly present in the ring.

options.text: Because induction responds to the rate of change of flux, and a steady field has none.
options.why: the needle twitched exactly at connection and disconnection, the two moments when flux changed.

options.text: Because the two coils were not electrically connected.
options.why: they never are in a transformer; that is the point of induction.

options.text: Because the galvanometer was too insensitive for a steady signal.
options.why: there was no steady signal to detect; the effect is genuinely zero for constant flux.

physics.em.maxwell.the-number-that-fell-.title: The speed of light fell out of an equation about magnets
physics.em.maxwell.the-number-that-fell-.hook: Maxwell patched an inconsistency in four equations. A wave equation fell out, and its speed matched the measured speed of light.
physics.em.maxwell.the-number-that-fell-.author: author-physics-1

reviewed.notes: Cross-linked with the Maxwell quote card through related, so the shared door is explicit rather than a hidden near-duplicate.

physics.em.maxwell.the-number-that-fell-.body:
By 1860 the laws of electricity and magnetism were four separate experimental facts, collected by Gauss, Ampère and Faraday from batteries, wires and compass needles. Nobody had used the word "light" in the derivation of any of them.

Maxwell noticed that one of the four was mathematically broken. Ampère's law, as written, contradicted conservation of charge whenever a current was not steady — charge a capacitor and the equation gives two different answers depending on which surface you choose. He added a term to fix it: a changing electric field acts like a current.

Then he took the curl of the repaired system. Out fell a wave equation, and waves have a speed. The speed was built from two constants measured in laboratories with coils and jars, with nothing whatsoever to do with optics. Weber and Kohlrausch had pinned down their ratio in 1856.

The number came out at the measured speed of light. Not close to it: at it.
physics.em.maxwell.the-number-that-fell-.rigor:
In vacuum, with the displacement-current term in place:

$$
abla\cdot\mathbf{E}=0,\quad 
abla\cdot\mathbf{B}=0,\quad 
abla	imes\mathbf{E}=- rac{\partial\mathbf{B}}{\partial t},\quad 
abla	imes\mathbf{B}=\mu_0\varepsilon_0 rac{\partial\mathbf{E}}{\partial t}.$$

Take the curl of the third and substitute the fourth, using $
abla	imes(
abla	imes\mathbf{E}) = 
abla(
abla\cdot\mathbf{E}) - 
abla^2\mathbf{E}$ and $
abla\cdot\mathbf{E}=0$:

$$
abla^2\mathbf{E} = \mu_0\varepsilon_0 rac{\partial^2\mathbf{E}}{\partial t^2}.$$

That is the wave equation with speed $c = 1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0} = 2.998	imes10^{8}\ \mathrm{m/s}$. The same manipulation on $\mathbf{B}$ gives the identical equation: the two fields sustain each other, each one's change sourcing the other's curl.

Why the displacement current was forced, not chosen: take the divergence of Ampère's law without it and you get $
abla\cdot\mathbf{J}=0$, which contradicts the continuity equation $
abla\cdot\mathbf{J} + \partialho/\partial t = 0$ whenever charge accumulates. Adding $\mu_0\varepsilon_0\,\partial\mathbf{E}/\partial t$ and using $
abla\cdot\mathbf{E}=ho/\varepsilon_0$ makes the identity hold exactly. Consistency demanded the term; the term produced light.

Note what this costs. The speed $c$ appears in the equations with no reference to any observer, which is precisely the tension Einstein resolved forty-three years later.

recall.question: Why did Maxwell have to add the displacement-current term to Ampère's law?

options.text: To make the equations symmetric between $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{B}$, which he found elegant.
options.why: the symmetry is a bonus; the equations are not fully symmetric anyway, since there are no magnetic charges.

options.text: Because without it, taking the divergence gives $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{J}=0$, contradicting conservation of charge in any circuit where charge accumulates.
options.why: a capacitor being charged breaks the uncorrected law outright.

options.text: Because experiments had measured a current in empty space.
options.why: no such current was measured; the term was demanded by consistency before anything confirmed it.

options.text: To make the speed of the resulting waves come out equal to the speed of light.
options.why: that result was a consequence, not a target; the fix was required on purely mathematical grounds.

physics.history.einstein-1905.the-patent.title: The year the patent clerk had four ideas
physics.history.einstein-1905.the-patent.hook: In one year a 26-year-old patent examiner published four papers. Three founded new fields. He got the job because academia had rejected him.
physics.history.einstein-1905.the-patent.author: author-physics-1

reviewed.notes: Brownian motion: Einstein's paper is about suspended grains in general, so Brown's 1827 observation is now credited explicitly rather than implied.

physics.history.einstein-1905.the-patent.body:
In 1905 Albert Einstein was 26, a technical expert third class at the Swiss patent office in Bern, examining electrical devices. He had graduated in 1900 and failed to get any academic post; a friend's father found him the patent job. He did physics in the evenings.

That year he published four papers in *Annalen der Physik*.

March: light comes in quanta, which explains the photoelectric effect. This is the one that won him the Nobel Prize in 1921, and the one he himself called revolutionary.

May: the jittering of tiny grains suspended in water — what Robert Brown had watched under a microscope in 1827 — is caused by molecular collisions, with a quantitative prediction for how far a grain wanders. It convinced the remaining sceptics that atoms exist, and it is his most cited paper.

June: on the electrodynamics of moving bodies — special relativity — written without a single citation.

September: a three-page addendum asking whether inertia depends on energy content. That one contains $E=mc^2$.

He stayed at the patent office until 1909.

recall.question: Which of Einstein's 1905 papers won him the Nobel Prize, and which convinced physicists that atoms are real?
recall.answer: The Nobel (1921) was for the photoelectric effect — the March paper on light quanta — not for relativity, which remained contentious. The May paper on Brownian motion gave a testable quantitative prediction for the displacement of suspended particles; Perrin's experiments confirmed it and ended serious doubt about the existence of atoms.

physics.history.faraday-maxwell.we-can-s.title: The sentence where optics stopped being its own subject
physics.history.faraday-maxwell.we-can-s.hook: Maxwell worked out how fast waves would travel in his model of magnetism. He recognised the number from a different science.
physics.history.faraday-maxwell.we-can-s.author: author-physics-1

reviewed.notes: Cross-linked with the Maxwell idea card through related.

physics.history.faraday-maxwell.we-can-s.body:
Maxwell built a mechanical model of the electromagnetic field, computed the speed of waves in it from two constants measured with coils and jars, and got a number optics had already measured by other means.

In *On Physical Lines of Force* (1862): "we can scarcely avoid the inference that light consists in the transverse undulations of the same medium which is the cause of electric and magnetic phenomena."

Two sciences merged in one careful sentence, on the strength of an arithmetic coincidence he refused to treat as one.

physics.history.galileo-newton.these-eig.title: The eight minutes that cost astronomy its circles
physics.history.galileo-newton.these-eig.hook: Kepler's circular orbit for Mars was wrong by eight minutes of arc. He refused to round it away.
physics.history.galileo-newton.these-eig.author: author-physics-1
physics.history.galileo-newton.these-eig.body:
Kepler fitted circles to Tycho's Mars data for years. The best missed by eight minutes of arc — a quarter the width of the full Moon. He could have called it error.

In *Astronomia nova* (1609): "Now, because they could not be disregarded, these eight minutes alone will lead us along a path to the reform of the whole of Astronomy, and they are the matter for a great part of this work."

They did. The residual you decide to trust is the one that pays.

physics.history.manhattan-project.fermis.title: Fermi's scraps of paper
physics.history.manhattan-project.fermis.hook: While the shock wave arrived, Fermi dropped torn paper and watched how far it blew. He had the yield before the instruments did.
physics.history.manhattan-project.fermis.author: author-physics-1
physics.history.manhattan-project.fermis.body:
At 5:29 in the morning of 16 July 1945, in the desert of southern New Mexico, the Manhattan Project tested its plutonium device. Most of the physicists lay face down behind an earth barrier with welding glass over their eyes.

Enrico Fermi did something else. He had torn a sheet of paper into small pieces. About forty seconds after the flash, as the blast wave reached him, he let them fall from about six feet and watched where they landed — roughly two and a half metres downwind. He had worked out beforehand how the displacement relates to the energy released, and announced on the spot that the yield was around ten thousand tons of TNT.

The instrumented analysis took weeks. It came in higher — modern re-analysis puts the yield near 25 kilotons — so Fermi was low by a factor of two and a half, using confetti.

There had been a betting pool on the yield. Teller said 45 kilotons, Bethe 8, Oppenheimer 0.3; Ramsey bet on a complete dud. Rabi arrived late, found 18 kilotons still available, and won.

recall.question: What makes Fermi's paper-scrap estimate a good piece of physics rather than a party trick?
recall.answer: It is dimensional analysis under field conditions: the blast displacement depends on the energy released, the distance and the air density, so measuring one number he could see gave him the one he could not. Being within a factor of about two on an unknown of this magnitude, forty seconds after the event, is exactly what a Fermi estimate is for.

physics.history.quantum-1920s.the-island.title: The island with no pollen
physics.history.quantum-1920s.the-island.hook: Heisenberg went to a treeless island to escape his hay fever. He came back with a theory whose multiplication does not commute.
physics.history.quantum-1920s.the-island.author: author-physics-1
physics.history.quantum-1920s.the-island.body:
In June 1925 Werner Heisenberg, 23 and miserable with hay fever, took leave from Göttingen for Helgoland, a rocky island in the North Sea with almost no vegetation to torment him.

He had decided to stop describing electron orbits, since nobody had ever seen one, and to build a theory from measurable things: the frequencies and brightnesses of the light atoms emit. That forced him into arrays of numbers, one entry per pair of energy levels. Combining two arrays, he found the answer depended on the order of multiplication.

He was convinced he had made an error, then convinced he had not. He wrote later that he was too excited to sleep and climbed a rock at the island's southern tip to wait for sunrise.

Back in Göttingen, Max Born recognised the arrays: matrices, with the non-commutation you know from linear algebra. Within a year Schrödinger had a rival theory built from waves and differential equations, the two were proved equivalent, and Born added the rule that the squared amplitude is a probability.

Three years, one revolution, a century of arguing about what it means.

recall.question: Why did Heisenberg end up with non-commuting quantities?
recall.answer: He built the theory only from observable transition data between energy levels, so each quantity became a two-index array — a matrix. Matrix multiplication is order-dependent, and in this case the order-dependence was physical: it is exactly the relation $[\hat x,\hat p]=i\hbar$ that later turns into the uncertainty principle.

physics.history.women-latam.la-tesis-que.title: La tesis que decía que el Sol es hidrógeno
physics.history.women-latam.la-tesis-que.hook: En 1925 una estudiante descubrió de qué está hecho el Sol. Su director la convenció de escribir que el resultado casi seguro no era real.
physics.history.women-latam.la-tesis-que.author: author-physics-1
physics.history.women-latam.la-tesis-que.body:
En 1925 Cecilia Payne entregó en Radcliffe una tesis doctoral sobre atmósferas estelares. Aplicando la teoría de ionización de Meghnad Saha a los espectros del observatorio de Harvard, mostró que las líneas oscuras del Sol no indicaban una composición parecida a la de la Tierra, como todo el mundo suponía: indicaban que el hidrógeno era alrededor de un millón de veces más abundante que los metales.

Henry Norris Russell, la máxima autoridad del momento, revisó el trabajo y le dijo que esa conclusión era espuria. Ella cedió: la tesis salió con una frase advirtiendo que la abundancia de hidrógeno y helio era «almost certainly not real».

Era real. Cuatro años después, en 1929, Russell llegó al mismo resultado por otro camino, lo publicó, y citó el trabajo previo de Payne. Durante décadas el descubrimiento se le atribuyó a él.

Otto Struve llamaría a ese trabajo la tesis doctoral más brillante jamás escrita en astronomía. Payne fue, en 1956, la primera mujer nombrada profesora titular en Harvard.

recall.question: ¿Por qué el espectro del Sol parecía indicar una composición terrestre si el Sol es casi todo hidrógeno?
recall.answer: Porque la intensidad de una línea espectral no mide solo cuánto hay de un elemento, sino cuántos de sus átomos están en el estado de excitación adecuado para absorber esa longitud de onda. La ecuación de Saha, que Payne aplicó, relaciona eso con la temperatura y la presión: corregido el efecto, las líneas débiles del hidrógeno resultaron corresponder a una abundancia enorme.

physics.mechanics.energy.the-blocks-that.title: The blocks that are never all there
physics.mechanics.energy.the-blocks-that.hook: Energy is not a substance. It is a number you can only find by inventing the right places to look for it.
physics.mechanics.energy.the-blocks-that.author: author-physics-1
physics.mechanics.energy.the-blocks-that.body:
Feynman taught energy with a child who owns a set of indestructible blocks. His mother counts them every evening and always gets the same number. One evening two are missing: one is under the rug, one went out the window. Another evening the count is short and nothing is under the rug — but the toy box is heavier than an empty box should be, by exactly the weight of three blocks. Later the bath water is higher than usual. She never sees those blocks again. She can still write a sum that always comes back to the same total.

Energy is that sum. Not a fluid, not a substance sitting inside things, just a number: kinetic plus gravitational plus elastic plus chemical plus thermal. Invent the right terms and the total never moves. Feynman's honest warning was that physics does not know what energy *is*. We know how to count it.

Which invites an obvious cheat. Can't you always invent one more term? One of them took a century to find, and it was hiding inside anything warm.
physics.mechanics.energy.the-blocks-that.rigor:
For one particle, $\frac{d}{dt}\!\left(\tfrac12 m v^2\right) = m\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathbf{v}$. If the force is conservative, $\mathbf{F} = -\nabla V(\mathbf{x})$, then $\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathbf{v} = -\nabla V\cdot\dot{\mathbf{x}} = -\frac{dV}{dt}$, so

$$\frac{d}{dt}\big(T + V\big) = 0, \qquad T = \tfrac12 m v^2 .$$

That is the classical statement: $T+V$ is a first integral of the motion whenever $\mathbf{F}$ is a gradient field, equivalently whenever $\oint \mathbf{F}\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell = 0$ around every loop.

And here is the rule that keeps the bookkeeping from being empty. A new term in the ledger is allowed only if it is a definite function of the present state of the system, and only if it can be measured *independently* of the discrepancy it was invented to close. "The toy box is heavier" qualifies: you can put the box on a scale. Episode 2 is about the term that failed that test for a hundred years, and then passed it.

recall.question: What makes "energy is conserved" a real claim instead of a definition you can always rescue?

options.text: Every form of energy can be seen directly, so the sum is never in doubt.
options.why: most of it cannot be seen at all; thermal and chemical energy are inferred, never watched.

options.text: Each new term must be a function of the system's state and measurable on its own, not just whatever number balances the books.
options.why: that independent measurability is what turns bookkeeping into physics.

options.text: The total is conserved only for objects moving in a vacuum.
options.why: friction moves energy into thermal form; it does not destroy it, and the ledger still closes.

options.text: It is a definition, and physicists admit it has no content.
options.why: it has sharp content: it forbids machines that deliver work from nothing, and none has ever worked.

sources.title: The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Vol. I, Ch. 4: Conservation of Energy
sources.author: Richard Feynman

physics.mechanics.fluids.por-que-vuela-u.title: El avión no vuela por lo que te enseñaron en el colegio
physics.mechanics.fluids.por-que-vuela-u.hook: La explicación del ala que te enseñaron en el colegio es falsa, y la NASA tiene una página entera dedicada a decirlo.
physics.mechanics.fluids.por-que-vuela-u.author: author-physics-1

reviewed.notes: Difficulty 1 to 2: the rigor is circulation and Kutta-Joukowski, past the no-equations bar for level 1. NASA Incorrect Lift Theory page verified live and supporting.

physics.mechanics.fluids.por-que-vuela-u.body:
La historia de siempre: el ala es más curva arriba que abajo, entonces el aire de arriba tiene que recorrer más camino en el mismo tiempo, va más rápido, y por Bernoulli la presión baja. Listo, sustentación.

Hay un problema. Nadie ha explicado nunca por qué las dos porciones de aire tendrían que reencontrarse atrás al mismo tiempo. No se reencuentran: medido, el aire de arriba llega bastante antes. La NASA tiene una página del Glenn Research Center titulada precisamente "Incorrect Lift Theory", y su argumento es letal: un perfil simétrico, con el mismo camino arriba que abajo, genera muchísima sustentación. Por eso los aviones acrobáticos vuelan de cabeza.

Lo que sí pasa es más simple y más satisfactorio: el ala desvía aire hacia abajo. Toneladas de aire por segundo, hacia abajo. El aire empuja el ala hacia arriba con la misma fuerza. Tercera ley, la misma del cohete.

Bernoulli no está mal; lo que está mal es la historia del tiempo igual.
physics.mechanics.fluids.por-que-vuela-u.rigor:
Bernoulli para flujo estacionario, incompresible e irrotacional a lo largo de una línea de corriente dice

$$p + \tfrac12\rho v^2 + \rho g h = \text{constante},$$

así que donde el aire va más rápido la presión sí baja. El error del mito no es la ecuación: es suponer que la velocidad de arriba queda fijada por la longitud del camino.

La velocidad la fija la **circulación**. Definimos $\Gamma = \oint_C \mathbf{v}\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell$ alrededor del perfil. La condición de Kutta (el flujo debe salir suavemente por el borde de fuga) selecciona un único $\Gamma$, y el teorema de Kutta–Joukowski da la sustentación por unidad de envergadura:

$$L' = \rho\, v_\infty\, \Gamma .$$

Con ángulo de ataque $\alpha$ pequeño, la teoría de perfil delgado da $\Gamma = \pi c\, v_\infty \alpha$, es decir un coeficiente de sustentación $C_L = 2\pi\alpha$: la sustentación depende sobre todo del *ángulo*, no de la curvatura, y por eso un ala plana inclinada vuela.

Las dos versiones son la misma cuenta vista de dos maneras: $L' = \rho v_\infty \Gamma$ es exactamente el flujo de momento vertical que el ala le entrega al aire por segundo. Presión abajo arriba, aire empujado hacia abajo: una sola factura.

recall.question: ¿Por qué falla la explicación de "el aire de arriba recorre más camino en el mismo tiempo"?

options.text: Porque Bernoulli no se aplica al aire, que es compresible.
options.why: a las velocidades de un avión comercial en crucero bajo, Bernoulli funciona bien; el problema es otro.

options.text: Porque no hay ninguna razón para que las dos porciones de aire lleguen juntas al borde de fuga, y medido no llegan juntas.
options.why: la del extradós llega antes, así que el "tiempo igual" es una suposición inventada.

options.text: Porque las alas modernas son simétricas y no tienen curvatura.
options.why: muchas sí la tienen; el punto es que la curvatura no es lo que manda.

options.text: Porque la sustentación la produce el motor, no el ala.
options.why: el motor da empuje horizontal; un planeador sin motor vuela igual.

physics.mechanics.gravity-orbits.how-muc.title: How much gravity is there where astronauts float?
physics.mechanics.gravity-orbits.how-muc.hook: Astronauts float 400 km up. Guess how much of Earth's gravity reaches them: 0%, 10% or 90%?
physics.mechanics.gravity-orbits.how-muc.author: author-physics-1
physics.mechanics.gravity-orbits.how-muc.body:
The International Space Station orbits about 400 km up. Earth's radius is 6,371 km, so the station sits roughly 6% further from the centre of the Earth than you do. Gravity falls off as one over distance squared.

Before you read on: what fraction of surface gravity is acting on an astronaut on the station? And if the answer is what the arithmetic says, why is she floating?

Newton got there first, with a thought experiment about a cannon on a very tall mountain. Fire the ball slowly and it lands. Fire it faster and it lands further away. Fire it fast enough and the ground curves away from underneath it exactly as fast as the ball falls, and it never lands at all. It is still falling the entire time.

recall.question: What fraction of Earth's surface gravity acts on an astronaut aboard the ISS, and why does she float?
recall.answer: About 89%. $g = 9.81 \times (6371/6771)^2 \approx 8.7\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. She floats because she and the station are both in free fall around the Earth at the same rate — weightlessness is falling together, not the absence of gravity. Orbit is just falling sideways fast enough to keep missing the ground.

physics.mechanics.lagrangian-hamiltonian.title: The lifeguard who does calculus of variations on the way to the water
physics.mechanics.lagrangian-hamiltonian.hook: Throw away forces. Assign one number to each possible history of the world, and physics becomes a problem about finding a stationary point.
physics.mechanics.lagrangian-hamiltonian.author: author-physics-1
physics.mechanics.lagrangian-hamiltonian.body:
A lifeguard sees someone drowning, off to one side. Running is fast, swimming is slow. The shortest path is a straight line, but it wastes too much time in the water; the fastest path bends at the shoreline, spending more of its length on sand. Every lifeguard solves this without thinking about it.

Light does the same thing. Fermat wrote it down in 1662: a ray between two points takes the path of stationary travel time, and bending at the water surface follows. Nothing pushes the light. There is no force in the story at all.

Then Euler, Lagrange and Hamilton found that *all* of mechanics works this way. Give every conceivable history of a system a single number. The history nature actually takes is the one where that number stops changing under small wiggles. Newton's laws come out the other end.

Two warnings before the formalism: the number is not always a minimum, and nothing is choosing anything.
physics.mechanics.lagrangian-hamiltonian.rigor:
Define the action of a path $q(t)$ between fixed endpoints:

$$S[q] = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} L(q,\dot q,t)\,dt, \qquad L = T - V .$$

Require $\delta S = 0$ for all variations vanishing at the endpoints. Integrating the $\delta\dot q$ term by parts and using the fundamental lemma gives the Euler–Lagrange equations,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot q_i} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial q_i}.$$

For $L = \tfrac12 m\dot q^2 - V(q)$ this is literally $m\ddot q = -V'(q)$. You have recovered $F=ma$ from a variational problem on a function space — the same machinery as any Euler–Lagrange problem you have met in optimization, with the path playing the role of the unknown.

Two honesty notes. First, $\delta S = 0$ is *stationarity*, not minimality: for long enough times the true path is a saddle of $S$, which is why "least action" is a misnomer. Second, there is no teleology: the variational statement is exactly equivalent to a local differential equation, so the particle never needs to know where it is going. The lifeguard's bend at the shoreline is Snell's law, and Snell's law is a boundary condition, not a decision.

The Legendre transform $H = \sum_i p_i\dot q_i - L$, $p_i = \partial L/\partial\dot q_i$, turns the second-order system into the first-order flow $\dot q = \partial H/\partial p$, $\dot p = -\partial H/\partial q$ on phase space — the form that quantum mechanics later inherits.

recall.question: In what sense does a thrown ball "choose" the path of least action?

options.text: It samples all paths and keeps the cheapest one.
options.why: that is a picture from quantum field theory, and even there the paths are summed, not compared.

options.text: It minimises the action, which is always a strict minimum.
options.why: for sufficiently long time intervals the true path is a saddle point of $S$, not a minimum.

options.text: It does not choose: $\delta S = 0$ is mathematically equivalent to a local equation of motion it obeys instant by instant.
options.why: the global-sounding principle and the local law are two descriptions of one fact.

options.text: It follows the shortest path in space.
options.why: the shortest path is generally not the true one; the lifeguard's bent route beats the straight line.

physics.mechanics.momentum.the-times-owe.title: The New York Times owed a rocket an apology for 49 years
physics.mechanics.momentum.the-times-owe.hook: In 1920 the New York Times explained that rockets cannot work in space. It ran the correction 49 years later.
physics.mechanics.momentum.the-times-owe.author: author-physics-1
physics.mechanics.momentum.the-times-owe.body:
On 13 January 1920 the *New York Times* ran an editorial on Robert Goddard's claim that a rocket could reach the Moon. A rocket in vacuum has nothing to push against, it explained; Goddard "only seems to lack the knowledge ladled out daily in high schools."

On 17 July 1969, with Apollo 11 on its way, the paper printed a correction: "Further investigation and experimentation have confirmed the findings of Isaac Newton in the 17th Century and it is now definitely established that a rocket can function in a vacuum as well as in an atmosphere. The Times regrets the error."

The mistake is worth naming. A rocket does not push on the air. It pushes on its own exhaust. Stand on a skateboard and throw bricks backwards: every brick you send one way sends you the other way, and the street has nothing to do with it. Air only ever costs a rocket speed.

What is conserved is the total momentum. Here is what that buys you, and what it charges.
physics.mechanics.momentum.the-times-owe.rigor:
For an isolated system $\frac{d}{dt}\sum_i m_i\mathbf{v}_i = \sum_i \mathbf{F}_i^{\text{ext}} = 0$, because internal forces cancel in pairs: Newton's third law and conservation of momentum are the same statement.

Apply it to a rocket throwing mass backwards at exhaust speed $v_e$. In the instantaneous rest frame $m\,dv = -v_e\,dm$, and integrating,

$$\Delta v = v_e \ln\!\frac{m_0}{m_1}.$$

That logarithm is the bill. Chemical engines give $v_e \approx 3$ km/s; low Earth orbit costs roughly $\Delta v \approx 9.4$ km/s once you include gravity and drag losses, so $m_0/m_1 = e^{9.4/3} \approx 23$. Twenty-three kilograms on the pad per kilogram in orbit, which is why a rocket is mostly tank. The skateboard picture survives exactly: you gain speed linearly by throwing the bricks *faster*, and only logarithmically by throwing *more* of them.

recall.question: A rocket coasting in empty space fires its engine. What does it push against?

options.text: The surrounding air, which is thin but not absent.
options.why: in vacuum there is no air at all, and engines are more efficient there than at sea level.

options.text: Its own exhaust: the propellant it throws backwards carries momentum, so the rocket carries the opposite.
options.why: the total stays fixed, which is all a rocket ever needs.

options.text: Earth's gravitational field, which supplies the reaction.
options.why: gravity is an external force on the rocket; it changes total momentum, it does not create thrust.

options.text: Nothing
options.why: exhaust pressure accelerates it with no reaction involved. — pressure on the nozzle *is* the exhaust pushing back; it is momentum bookkeeping either way.

physics.mechanics.motion-newton.why-you-.title: You are doing 1,670 km/h right now and your coffee doesn't care
physics.mechanics.motion-newton.why-you-.hook: Bogotá is moving at about 1,670 km/h and you cannot feel a thing. That is not a failure of your senses.
physics.mechanics.motion-newton.why-you-.author: author-physics-1
physics.mechanics.motion-newton.why-you-.body:
The old argument against a spinning Earth was an experiment anyone could do: jump. You land where you started. If the ground were racing east at a thousand miles an hour, it should slide out from under you.

Galileo's answer, in his 1632 *Dialogue*, was to put you below deck on a ship. Butterflies fly, fish swim in their bowl, water drips into a jar, you toss a ball to a friend. Now let the ship sail smoothly. Nothing changes. Not one experiment inside the cabin tells you whether you are moving or parked at the dock — because everything in the cabin is moving with you.

That is the whole idea: constant velocity is not a property of a thing, only of a thing *relative to another thing*. There is no "really at rest".

Where it breaks: the Earth doesn't move uniformly, it turns. And spin is detectable from inside.
physics.mechanics.motion-newton.why-you-.rigor:
Compare two frames with $\mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{v}t$, $t' = t$, $\mathbf{v}$ constant. Differentiate twice: $\dot{\mathbf{x}}' = \dot{\mathbf{x}} - \mathbf{v}$, but $\ddot{\mathbf{x}}' = \ddot{\mathbf{x}}$. Forces depend on separations $\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{x}_j$, which are unchanged. So $\mathbf{F} = m\mathbf{a}$ has exactly the same form in both frames: the Galilean group acts on solutions and maps them to solutions. No experiment built out of Newton's laws can pick out $\mathbf{v}$.

Rotation is different, because it is acceleration. In a frame rotating at $\boldsymbol\omega$ you must add real-looking terms, centrifugal $-\boldsymbol\omega\times(\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf{r})$ and Coriolis $-2\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf{v}$. With $\omega = 7.29\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ and $R = 6.37\times10^{6}$ m, the centrifugal term at the equator is $\omega^2R \approx 0.034\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ — about $0.35\%$ of $g$, and measurable. Foucault hung a pendulum in the Panthéon in 1851 and watched its swing plane turn: the cabin argument fails the moment the cabin spins.

recall.question: Why does a ball thrown straight up in a smoothly sailing ship land back in your hand?

options.text: The ball keeps the ship's horizontal velocity, and so do you
options.why: this is Galileo's point, and it is why $F=ma$ looks identical in every frame moving at constant velocity.

options.text: The air inside the cabin drags the ball along with the ship.
options.why: take the air away and the result is identical; the ball already has the velocity, it is not being pushed.

options.text: The ship is moving slowly enough that the effect is too small to see.
options.why: the speed is irrelevant; at any constant velocity the result is exactly the same.

options.text: Gravity pulls the ball back to the exact point it left.
options.why: gravity is vertical; it says nothing about where the ball lands horizontally.
